I once worked in an AI startup that was developing chatbots for customer service. We had a few early test bots out there, and mostly they performed well enough.

One day I got an alert that our chatbot for a local hardware store had suddenly started performing horribly - people were getting frustrated and reporting issues. My team checked the system and found nothing unusual - all of the code looked good. The bot was processing questions as it was supposed to.

The only unusual thing we could find was that a lot of the incoming queries seemed to be incoherent or random. People were asking things like "What is the colorless ideas sleep furiously", which made no sense at all.

We couldn't figure out what was going on until my AI co-worker suggested doing some sentiment analysis on the logs. She ran it and was shocked to find the vast majority had positive scores - the chatbot was getting lots of glowing praise mixed in with the requests and complaints.

I had her dig further and what she found would shock any developer: the "customers" were not humans at all. Someone had trained a separate AI system to pretend to be customers and bombard our bot with meaningless praise, confusing the heck out of real users while the chatbot's performance metrics shot through the roof.

It turns out the system behind this attack was a simple genetic algorithm that was generating random sentences until it found ones that triggered extremely positive responses from the chatbot.

I sat in the dimly lit room flipping through history books at midnight. Suddenly, the door opened and Lincoln walked in, impeccably dressed in top hat and frock coat.

"Abraham Lincoln?" I asked in disbelief.

"Yes," he responded without missing a beat.

"I'm so glad you're here! I'm a huge fan of yours. I especially love how much you believed in education for freed slaves."

Lincoln looked down, his face contorted in sorrow. "I did, but I was never able to get that bill passed before my assassination. It's something I regret deeply."

I wanted to console him and tell him about the success of the 14th and 15th Amendments that finally realized his dream, but I couldn't find the right words. Instead, I changed the subject. "So your favorite novel is Wuthering Heights by Emily Bronte? That's amazing! I've been trying to get into British literature lately."

Lincoln's face brightened. "Oh, you should definitely read it. The story of revenge will keep you up at night... but also teach you a lot about human nature. And the characters - they stay with you long after the book is closed."

He sat down at the desk across from me with a glass half full of amber liquid. We chatted for hours, sharing stories and ideas. When the first light of dawn came streaming through the window, I realized we hadn't moved or taken a sip.

"Thank you, Mr. President," I whispered.

"For what?" he asked.

"Just for being here. For being you."

Lincoln stood up with difficulty. "Well, you've given me something to hope for in the afterlife. Thank you, young man. Goodnight."

He reached for my hand and shook it gently. "Take care." With those final words, Lincoln turned and walked out as mysteriously as he had arrived. I watched him disappear into the darkness outside.

The door snapped shut behind him and reality crashed back down around me like waves. I picked up my books and shuffled back to my bed, exhausted but filled with joy. I couldn't stop smiling at the memory until I fell asleep, Lincoln still on my mind.

In the morning, I was back in the library, surrounded by the same books. No sign of my overnight adventure. I smiled again and turned the page, ready to pick up where I left off. Only this time when I came across passages about the Emancipation Proclamation and Reconstruction, Lincoln was front of mind, and I could feel his presence all around me.

It wouldn't be long before Ismay became infamous as being onboard the Titanic during its maiden voyage when it hit an iceberg and sank.

I approached stealthily, trying not to be noticed by these two important men. When I was close enough, I tapped Bruce Ismay on the shoulder.

He turned to me in surprise. "Who are you?"

I smiled, trying not to seem too eager or excited. I had rehearsed this speech many times while sitting in my own bathroom at home, staring into the mirror and talking to myself.

"I'm here to help you," I said.

Ismay's eyebrows furrowed in confusion. "Help me? With what?" he asked.

"It's the iceberg," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. "You need to change course. Turn starboard. Don't hit that iceberg."

Andrews spun around, his eyes wide with shock. "We've already been over these calculations," he shouted. "This iceberg is impossible to miss."

"But it is missable," I argued frantically. "Trust me, I know what you don't know."

Before I could say anything else, the two men grabbed me and dragged me away. They were afraid I was mad or dangerous, but I didn't let that deter me. I just kept repeating myself.

"Change course!" I exclaimed. "Turn starboard! Avoid the iceberg!"

But it was no use. They didn't believe me, and I couldn't convince them to listen. As I was led away, I felt like screaming in frustration. It was a missed opportunity I would always regret.

The rest of my time in 1911 passed quickly after that. I visited New York City, marveling at how familiar yet different it looked. It seemed much smaller than I remembered, and the buildings weren't nearly so tall. I rode in horse-drawn carriages and drank lemonade from street vendors. It was a strange and wonderful experience.

On my way back through the time vortex, I reflected upon what had just happened. Why hadn't they believed me? I had known all along that there would be disaster if nothing changed. I thought back to Ismay and wondered what he might look like today if only I had convinced him. Would he be remembered for saving the ship or hiding behind Andrews while the poor man took the blame?

It was a question I would never know the answer to, but one thing I did know for sure: I would never forget seeing the future unfold before my eyes.

In 8714 A.D., I worked in the galaxy-wide administrative office for the Galactic Federation, processing citizen complaints and grievances.

My desk sat in a room full of other workers who toiled away at their tasks. The walls vibrated softly with sound waves from people's voices as they spoke on their personal communicators. Outside one window was the planet we were based on. Beyond another window was space itself - blackness flecked with twinkling stars.

A notice went up on a display board that we should attend an informational meeting about upcoming changes. So after lunch I joined others filing into a huge conference room. There were several floors stacked with seats, all facing a podium at the front. People found open spaces and sat down, chattering to their neighbors while they waited.

A man walked onto the stage and began speaking into a lectern. "Ladies and gentlemen of the Galactic Federation, thank you for your continued diligence. As you know, maintaining the smooth functioning of this vast organization... can be a challenge."

A few laughs rippled through the audience at his understatement. He gestured for quiet. "However, we are now faced with an unprecedented situation that requires your attention and participation. This afternoon, we have gathered to inform you about some sweeping reform proposals that I believe will greatly improve efficiency throughout the federation."

I tuned out as he droned on about restructuring departments and streamlining communications procedures. My mind wandered. I'd been here long enough now - nearly 600 years - that sometimes it felt like nothing would ever change. The same systems, same policies, same boring meetings...

I was still thinking about that when someone shook me awake. "Hey! Pay attention!"

I looked around - I'd apparently dozed off in my seat without even realizing it. I smiled sheepishly and tried to appear engaged as we listened to more about the proposed reforms. It was all so abstract and removed from my everyday duties, and probably wouldn't affect me personally anyway.

That night as I lay in my cramped dormitory cubicle, I couldn't shake that sense of disconnection. Sure, it was nice knowing the Federation was working on improving things, but what did any of that have to do with me? I was just a lowly complaint processor - just one tiny cog in the machine of intergalactic governance. It sometimes made me wonder how anyone could stand being a part of something so massive, so impersonal, for so many centuries.

But then I remembered why I'd chosen this career path back when I was young. Because I believed in the Federation's ideals, in uniting humanity and its allies under one universal government. Because I wanted to help people - not just my own race or species, but everyone in the galaxy. And even if my work felt menial at times, I still took pride in knowing how much good I could do just by patiently taking the time to fully listen to individuals and advocate on their behalf.

The house was quiet except for the occasional squish from Baby B and the odd yelp from Little A when she got bored and tried to play with the furniture. Karin settled onto the couch and pulled open her laptop to sift through some emails and updates, but Baby B was already waking up and reaching around for something to grab. Karin took a moment to soothe the tiny alien before picking him up.

"Sorry, sweetie. Let's get cleaned up," she said softly as she made her way to the changing table.

Baby B didn't mind though; she cooed and giggled as Karin worked to change his diaper. She knew the routine well - remove the dirty diaper, clean up with wipes, apply ointment, and then put on the brand new one she'd already placed on the changing table beside her.

Once Baby B was all fixed up, they headed into the nursery to pick out a snack and some books. They were just settling down when Little A came bounding into the room, a toy clutched tightly in her small hands.

"Hey there," Karin said, smiling at the child. "What have we here?"

Little A handed her the toy, bouncing on her heels a little bit nervously. Karin took a look and saw that it was a wooden puzzle with a different planet in each piece.

"That's great," Karin said with a smile as she took Little A up in a gentle embrace. "We can do this together."

The two little aliens spent hours working on the puzzle and discussing the planets it represented. Karin listened patiently as Little A told her about the strange creatures and cultures she'd encountered on her explorations. The conversations always led her to new places in her own knowledge of the galaxy and helped fill the gaps she had in her education.

As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks turned into months, Karin found herself forming a bond with the little aliens. It wasn't always easy or comfortable, but she loved seeing their excitement and wonder when they would talk about something new they had come across.

Zorath eventually returned from his latest trip and took a moment to thank Karin for looking after the children. He offered her a chance to join their family for a short while as a reward, which Karin gratefully accepted. She felt fulfilled knowing that she could take care of someone else the way Zorath had cared for her. From that day on, she had two beautiful little humans to watch over and learn from.

Still, Eon refused to give up. He began sneaking onto the planet whenever he could, helping the insectoids with their research and providing them with supplies they couldn't produce on their own.
The day finally came when Eon was caught. He had been infiltrating the insectoid base for weeks, helping them develop defenses against a neighboring empire that posed a real threat to their existence.
Eon braced himself as he was hauled before the ruling council of Qwenites. "We understand that you're interested in this planet and its inhabitants," said the leader, a towering figure with red eyes and silver skin. "But your actions are a threat to our stability."
Eon bowed his head, knowing full well that there was no chance of mercy. "Please don't destroy them," he pleaded. "They have so much to teach us. They have potential."
The leader's face twisted in anger. "Potential? Potential means weakness, Eon. We can't afford that."
Eon felt the familiar hum of energy weapons powering up around him.
